newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia to set up depository for securities.
newsitem.headline: Croatia to set up depository for securities.

text.p: Croatia will set up a central depositary agency this week to add some of the missing blocks to its capital market, the state securities commission said on Monday.

"This is planned for February 28 and although the exact ownership structure is still not quite certain, there should be no problems over going ahead with it," head of the securities commission Ivica Smiljan told Reuters.
He could not give a timetable for when the agency would start operating in earnest.
Members of the Zagreb bourse, banks and brokers, which have been invited to subscribe equity in the depository, are expected to give their final word on the founding any time, Smiljan said.
The move, widely hailed by market participants, comes five months after the market watchdog itself was set up under securities legislation passed almost a year ago.
The depository will take charge of securities custody and transfer and is also expected to speed up lengthy clearing and settlement, according to a draft put forward to prospective shareholders.
Difficulties with these procedures have been blamed repeatedly by traders and analysts for turning investors away from Croatia's expanding stock market.

"The agency is supposed to be organised according to top world standards. It will increase the confidence of foreign investors which in turn should help the market no end," said Vladimir Puskaric of the Zagreb Stock Exchange.
The depository will eventually also have a guarantee fund to be activated in case of a default by any market participant, be it in payment or delivery of the purchased securities.
Settlement now takes seven days from each transaction and traders welcomed a proposed shortening.
"We cannot wait for it to be cut to five or even three days from each deal. If other things are also resolved, we can really begin to make headway," one of them said.
In the absence of a central register, several institutions have until now kept track of bonds and government securities.
At the same time, individual firms were responsible for issuing ownership certificates to buyers of shares and apart from a few were often accused of dragging their feet.
In a volatile market, prices have been known to soar after a deal and then drop again to below the bargain price, all before ownership papers were handed over.
"It is very practical for all of these things to be taken care of under one roof," Puskaric said.
It is estimated that up to $12 million will be required for the running of the depositary agency and for equipment over the next five years.
Part of these funds are expected be secured from a World Bank loan to prop up capital market reforms, analysts said.
It is to be founded with four million kuna ($668,000) equity, of which 61 percent will be owned by the Republic of Croatia and 15 percent by the state-run central payments bureau (ZAP).

Zagrebacka Banka, whose brokerage was the most active of all traders in 1996, may control seven percent and rest will be split between the Zagreb Stock Exchange, an over-the-counter market in Varazdin and other private banks and brokerages.
But Smiljan said the government planned to privatise the agency fully within three years from its founding.
"The government will gradually shed its holding, but ZAP will not be able to increase its own and it may even be dismantled by then," he said. ($ = 5.980 Croatian Kuna)
